Our formidable system of flight, a machine that’s constantly in motion and choreographed to the minute, has backups built in. Even before the blue wave crashed over Republicans and Democrats emerged with a commanding majority in the Senate, the rumblings for Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to step aside were there. articles.title: Scott Colom Is Mississippi’s First Black Senator in 150 Years
articles.author: Adam Serwer
articles.summary: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. One fall afternoon in Liberty, Mississippi, in 1961, a white Democratic former congressman and state legislator named E. H. Hurst shot Herbert Lee in the head. Hurst was angry that Lee, who was Black, had been trying to register other Black Mississippians to vote. An all-white jury accepted Hurst’s claim that he had acted in self-defense because Lee came at him with a tire iron. Donald Trump, now the sitting president of the United States, was 15 years old. This was how “negro law” worked in Jim Crow Mississippi, which was essentially a police state. Although many laws were race-neutral in their language, “in a society in which race mattered above all else, ‘negro law’ determined who was punished for what,” the historian Neil McMillen wrote in Dark Journey , his 1989 history of Mississippi. In the 1940s, the NAACP was “virtually forced to operate underground,” because in 1920, the state legislature had made it illegal to “possess or distribute” material that would “disturb relations between the races.” As late as 1961, a white man could shoot a Black man in broad daylight and get away with it.
